standard.title: Identity shaped by language, culture and values — evaluate
standard.description: reflect on and evaluate how their own and others' identity is shaped by language(s), culture(s), attitudes, beliefs and values, and how these affect ways of communicating
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can reflect on and explain how their own and others' identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes and values, and can identify stereotyping risks in intercultural interaction (AC9LCH8U04). They have examined cultural participation and communication adaptation. They have not yet evaluated the impact of globalisation on cultural identity, analysed how title and address conventions reflect cultural values, or reflected on non-verbal cultural behaviour and dress codes as communication.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students reflect on and evaluate how their own and others' identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes, beliefs and values — including the impact of globalisation, loan words, title conventions, non-verbal behaviour, and the ongoing relationship between language change and cultural identity.

nodes.label: Evaluating globalisation's impact on language and identity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate how globalisation has shaped modern target language use — including loan words, internet language, and cultural change — and reflect on the impact on their own identity and beliefs.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least three examples of globalisation's influence on the target language (loan words, internet language, or cultural change) and evaluate the impact of at least one on cultural identity.
nodes.typical_width: Examine the impact of globalisation on cultural change and language; explore loan words and internet language in modern target language use; reflect on how globalisation has affected own identity and beliefs; evaluate the relationship between language change and cultural maintenance.
wider: Research how a specific wave of globalisation — media, technology, trade — has affected target language vocabulary and cultural practices, and evaluate whether the changes strengthen or challenge cultural identity
Compare own family's language practices across generations — identify where globalisation has changed language use and what this reveals about identity negotiation across time
nodes.hinge_reason: Evaluating globalisation's impact is the conceptual prerequisite for the most sophisticated identity reflection the strand requires. Students who have only described language-culture connections cannot evaluate the dynamic, contested relationship between language change, cultural identity and globalisation.

response_modes.reason: Evaluating globalisation's impact requires students to distinguish between language change as cultural enrichment and language change as cultural erosion — a genuinely contested question. Explicit frameworks for evaluating impact, rather than only describing it, build the critical analytical capacity the descriptor requires.

success_criteria: Identifies at least three examples of globalisation's influence on the target language
Evaluates the impact of at least one on cultural identity with reasoned argument

nodes.label: Title conventions and non-verbal cultural behaviour
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how title and address conventions in the target language reflect cultural values of respect and formality, and how non-verbal cultural behaviour — dress codes, body language, space — affects communication.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain at least two title or address conventions in the target language and their cultural significance, and identify at least two non-verbal cultural behaviours that affect communication across cultural contexts.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how titles indicate respect and formality in target language versus Australian culture; compare address and title conventions across cultural contexts; examine how non-verbal cultural behaviour — dress codes, personal space, silence, volume — affects communication; discuss how these behaviours may be misinterpreted.
wider: Compare title and address conventions across multiple target language community contexts — identify where conventions vary within the target language world and what this reveals about regional or generational cultural change
Research a specific non-verbal behaviour that differs across target language and English-speaking contexts — explain the cultural logic on both sides and discuss the miscommunication risks

response_modes.reason: Title, address and non-verbal conventions must be understood across varied social contexts — professional, familial, formal, informal — before students can generalise their understanding. Varied cultural context encounters build the nuanced awareness the descriptor requires.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Title and non-verbal convention analysis has direct practical relevance for background learners navigating between cultural contexts. Width investment here builds the conscious cross-cultural awareness that transforms lived experience into articulable intercultural competence.
success_criteria: Explains at least two title or address conventions and their cultural significance
Identifies at least two non-verbal cultural behaviours that affect communication across cultural contexts

nodes.label: Evaluating own multilingual identity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate how their own multilingual and multicultural identity has been shaped by the languages, cultures, attitudes and values they have encountered, and how this shapes their ways of communicating.
nodes.minimum_width: Produce a reflective evaluation of at least ten sentences examining how at least two languages or cultural contexts have shaped their identity and communication style.
nodes.typical_width: Reflect on how own identity is shaped by languages, cultures, attitudes and values encountered daily; evaluate how multilingual background shapes communication choices; reflect on the protocols required for culturally authentic communication with diverse communities including First Nations Australians.
wider: Produce an extended reflective account of own language and cultural identity journey — tracing how it has developed, what has shaped it, and how it continues to evolve

Compare own multilingual identity experience with that of a peer, parent, or community member from a different generation — identify what has changed in how identity is navigated across language communities and discuss what has driven the change

response_modes.reason: Multilingual identity evaluation integrates globalisation analysis (node 1) and cultural behaviour understanding (node 2) into a full, personally-grounded synthesis. The teaching investment is in creating a genuinely reflective, non-prescriptive environment where students can examine their own identity honestly — including tensions, contradictions and ongoing negotiations — rather than producing a tidy, resolved account.

success_criteria: Produces a reflective evaluation examining how at least two languages or cultural contexts have shaped own identity
Connects identity reflection to specific communication style choices or adaptations
